nameStory: The seaside dragonlet gets its name from its love of coastal habitats where most other dragonflies fear to venture. While other dragonflies stick to freshwater ponds and streams, this little pioneer heads straight for the salty marshes and brackish waters near the ocean. The 'dragonlet' part reflects its relatively small size compared to the bigger, more familiar dragonflies.
description: The seaside dragonlet is a small, delicate dragonfly that's perfectly at home in coastal environments where most of its relatives can't survive. These compact fliers typically measure about 1-1.5 inches long with a wingspan around 2 inches. Males often show reddish coloration on their bodies, while females tend to be more yellowish or amber-colored. You'll spot them darting low over salt marshes and coastal ponds, their four wings catching the sunlight as they hunt for tiny flying insects.

idTips.label: Coastal habitat preference
idTips.description: Found exclusively near saltwater or brackish environments - if you see a small dragonfly over a salt marsh or coastal pond, it's likely this species

idTips.label: Small, compact size
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller than most dragonflies you'll encounter, with a delicate build that feels almost fragile compared to larger skimmers

idTips.label: Male coloration
idTips.description: Adult males develop a warm reddish or orange-red color on their abdomen and thorax, most vivid in bright sunlight

idTips.label: Low flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies close to the water surface in short, darting movements rather than the high, sweeping flights of larger dragonflies

idTips.label: Clear wings
idTips.description: Wings are mostly clear and colorless, sometimes with a faint amber tint at the base, and make a soft buzzing sound in flight

habitat: Look for seaside dragonlets in coastal salt marshes, brackish ponds, and shallow lagoons throughout coastal New England. They thrive in areas where saltwater mixes with fresh water, including tidal pools, salt pannes, and the edges of estuaries. You'll often find them sharing habitat with salt-tolerant plants like salt marsh aster and cordgrass.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, with early individuals appearing in May along the warmest coastal areas. Look for fresh, newly-emerged adults with bright colors.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs during summer months when adults are most abundant and actively breeding. This is the best time to observe their territorial behaviors and mating flights.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into early fall, though numbers decline as temperatures drop. Late-season individuals may appear more worn with faded colors.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off with the first hard frosts, though the species overwinters as aquatic nymphs hidden in marsh sediments and will emerge again the following year.

funFact: The seaside dragonlet is the only dragonfly in the entire Western Hemisphere that can actually breed in full-strength seawater - its aquatic nymphs can survive and develop in salt concentrations that would kill almost any other freshwater insect!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small dragonflies, but habitat is the dead giveaway - if you're seeing small dragonflies over salt marshes or brackish water, you've found seaside dragonlets. Remember: 'Salt marsh = seaside dragonlet' since other small dragonflies avoid salty environments.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - while called a 'dragonlet,' this is still a full dragonfly, just smaller than most. The term 'dragonlet' is used for several genera of compact dragonflies, but doesn't indicate they're a different type of insect.
compareHints: Since this is the only Erythrodiplax species in New England, compare it to other small skimmers in the family Libellulidae. Seaside dragonlets are distinguished by their exclusive coastal habitat preference and salt tolerance, while similar small dragonflies like eastern pondhawks or blue dashers stick to freshwater environments. The habitat difference is so reliable that location alone can often confirm identification.
